thesis: This episode argues that successful companies often operate as 'clones' of their competitors, copying their business models while adding unique strengths like cost discipline or genuine product improvement. It emphasizes that true success comes from being a 'good cloner' rather than a 'good cloner,' and that companies like Microsoft, Walmart, and Coca-Cola have built great businesses by cloning each other while maintaining their own distinct advantages.

claims.claim: Microsoft is described as a clone business that has built a great business despite not being a good cloner.
claims.quote: Microsoft is a clone business. They have spent tens of billions of dollars, probably spending tens of billions of dollars every year. And the only things that make money are office. So Word is cloned from WordPerfect.

claims.claim: Walmart is called the ultimate cloner that copied Sears and Kmart models but added incredible cost discipline.
claims.quote: If you look at someone like Walmart, Sam Walton, the ultimate cloner. He spent an incredible amount of time in his competitor stores. And in fact, if you read his autobiography made in America, it will just show you that for the first 20 years of Walmart's existence, Walmart had no new ideas.

claims.claim: Coca-Cola and Pepsi are cited as highly successful companies that cloned each other.
claims.quote: Coca-Cola, look at Pepsi. Highly successful, they cloned it. So actually, I think cloning is very powerful because there is room for more than one.

claims.claim: Bing is mentioned as cloning Google, though the speaker notes it is not Google.
claims.quote: And Bing, the full form of Bing is, but it's not Google. So Bing is cloning Google. and just go on and on. And they're not even a good cloner. It takes about 5, 6, 7 versions for them to get it right.

claims.claim: Pepsi is described as a highly successful company that cloned Coca-Cola.
claims.quote: Coca-Cola, look at Pepsi. Highly successful, they cloned it. So actually, I think cloning is very powerful because there is room for more than one.

claims.claim: Sears is mentioned as a model that Walmart copied, though no specific view is given on Sears itself.
claims.quote: But they pretty much copied the Sears and came out model. So they had a slight tweak to the other models. Coca-Cola, look at Pepsi. Highly successful, they cloned it.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Procter & Gamble has a principle of never marketing anything unless what they say is true and is genuinely an improvement.
claims.quote: I'm pretty sure the people at Procter & Gamble have never read Hawkins because the company three dates Hawkins. But PNG has a principle. They have a principle that they will never market anything unless whatever they are saying is true and it is genuinely an improvement.

claims.claim: The speaker states that over 100 years of history, Procter & Gamble has found that you cannot put lipstick on a pig; if you have a substandard product and dress it up, it doesn't do well.
claims.quote: probably over 100 years of history of marketing, everything, and they're the gods of marketing, is you cannot, in effect, put lipstick on a pig, okay? So if you have a substandard product and dress it up, what happens is the human attractor field just see straight through that, and those products don't do well.

claims.claim: The speaker concludes that Procter & Gamble really understands that at the core, and they are playing off Hawkins, even if they may not realize it.
claims.quote: And so the attractive is I would say that someone like P&G really understands that at the core. And I think they may not realize it, but they really are playing off Hawkins.
